kilogram.title: A kilogram is not a newton
steps:
Pick up a bag of rice. What you feel pressing into your hand is not the rice's mass. It is the Earth pulling the rice down: its weight.

A bracket feels the same thing. It does not care how much stuff hangs from it; it cares how hard that stuff pulls. So every calculation in this path starts by turning a mass into a force.

= ·

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

W
the weight: a force, in newtons (N)
m
the mass: how much stuff, in kilograms (kg)
g
how hard the Earth pulls on each kilogram, in m/s²

In one sentence

The weight is the mass times how hard the Earth pulls on every kilogram of it.

Where it comes from

A force is what it takes to make a mass speed up. Newton's second law says exactly how much: force = mass × acceleration. Let go of anything and it falls, speeding up by 9.81 m/s every second. That acceleration is g.

So the pull of the Earth on a mass m is m · g. When the bag sits still in your hand, your hand pushes up with exactly that force. That is why the bag feels heavy.

The newton is defined by the same law: one newton is the force that speeds up one kilogram by one metre per second, every second. That is why a kilogram weighs about ten newtons here on Earth.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. kg × m/s² is, by definition, a newton. If your units do not end in N, you have not found a force.
  • Size. The force in newtons is about ten times the mass in kilograms. A bag of a few kilograms weighs a few tens of newtons. If your answer is not roughly ten times the mass, stop and look again.

The trap

Writing the mass where the force is asked. "The load is 25 kg, so the force is 25 N" is wrong by a factor of about ten, and it is the most common first mistake. The units catch it before any grader does: kg is not N.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket carries a mass of 25 kg.

W = m · g = 25 × 9.81 = 245.25 N

About ten times 25, as it should be.

Your turn, half done

A sack of 18 kg hangs from the same hook. Here m = 18 kg and g = 9.81 m/s². Multiply them: what is its weight?

N

W = 18 × 9.81 = 176.58 N. About ten times the mass.

Your turn

A chain hoist and the engine block it holds have a mass of 32 kg together. What force do they put on the beam above them?

N

W = m · g = 32 × 9.81 = 313.92 N.

Check yourself

A crate's label says 24 kg. Which of these is the force it puts on the shelf?

About ten times the mass, in newtons. A kilogram is a mass, not a force, so (a) answers the wrong question. And (c) forgot g: it is the number of the mass wearing the unit of a force.
What you can do now: turn any mass into the force it pulls with. In the wall bracket challenge, this is step 1.

units.title: Units that carry you
steps:
Engineers on a drawing board work in newtons and millimetres, and so does this path. Not because metres are wrong, but because of what comes out at the other end.

A drawing is dimensioned in millimetres. A load is a force in newtons. Keep both, and a stress comes out in N/mm², which is exactly a megapascal (MPa): the unit every steel is sold in. No conversion, no chance to slip by a factor of a million.

(N·mm) = (N·m) × 1 000

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

M
a moment: a force times a distance

In one sentence

A metre is a thousand millimetres, so a newton-metre is a thousand newton-millimetres.

Where it comes from

A moment is a force times a distance (lesson 3 shows why). Change the unit of the distance and nothing physical changes: the same spanner, the same push. Only the number changes.

Measure the same distance in millimetres instead of metres and the number becomes a thousand times bigger, because each millimetre is a thousand times smaller. The force has not moved, so the moment's number grows by the same thousand.

Check it makes sense

  • A smaller unit gives a bigger number. N·mm are small, so a moment in N·mm is a big number: hundreds of thousands, for a bracket.
  • One family per calculation. Millimetres with millimetres, metres with metres. Mix them inside one line and the answer is out by a thousand, silently.

The trap

Dividing when you should multiply. Going from N·m to N·mm the number must get bigger. If yours got smaller, flip it. The same goes for kN to N: a kilonewton is a thousand newtons, so the number grows.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket's root moment is 107 910 N·mm. In N·m the number is a thousand times smaller: the same moment.

The final challenge accepts your answer in either unit, N·m or N·mm, kN or N. What it cannot do is fix a calculation that mixed them halfway through.

Your turn, half done

A spanner puts a moment of 48.6 N·m on a bolt. Multiply by a thousand: what is that in N·mm?

N·mm

48.6 × a thousand = 48 600 N·mm. Bigger number, smaller unit, same moment.

Your turn

A load cell reads 1.75 kN. What is that force in newtons?

N

A kilonewton is a thousand newtons: 1.75 kN = 1750 N.

Check yourself

Which of these is exactly the same as 1 MPa?

1 N/mm². A megapascal is a million pascals, and a square metre is a million square millimetres, so the two millions cancel. That is the reason to work in N and mm: stresses come out in MPa by themselves.
What you can do now: move between N and kN, N·m and N·mm, without losing a factor of a thousand, and say why a stress in N/mm² is already in MPa.

turning-force.title: The turning force
steps:
Why is a door handle on the side away from the hinges? Try pushing a door right beside its hinge: you push hard and it barely moves. Push at the handle and one finger will do.

The force is the same. What changed is how far from the pivot you pushed. Engineers have a name for force-with-distance: the moment. It is what bends a bracket, and it is the number the rest of this branch is built on.

= ·

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

M
the moment: how hard the force twists, in N·mm
F
the force, in newtons (N)
d
the lever arm: the distance from the pivot to the force's line, in mm

In one sentence

How hard a force twists is the force times how far it is from the pivot.

Where it comes from

Archimedes wrote this rule down more than two thousand years ago, and you can feel it on a see-saw. A child far from the middle balances a heavier adult sitting close in, and they balance exactly when force × distance is the same on both sides. It is not the force that has to match, and not the distance: it is their product.

That product is the moment. A long spanner turns a stuck nut because it makes d big, so a normal push makes a big M.

One detail matters: d is measured square to the force, from the pivot to the line the force acts along. Push along the spanner, towards the nut, and d is zero: nothing turns, however hard you push.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. N × mm = N·mm. A moment is never in N alone, and never in mm alone.
  • Double the force, double the moment. Double the arm, double the moment. Nothing is squared here.
  • Zero arm, zero moment. Pushing on the hinge does nothing: check your picture agrees.

The trap

Measuring the arm from the wrong point. On a bracket the pivot is the centre of the bolt pattern, where the bracket is held, not the face of the column and not the end of the plate. A wrong starting point gives a wrong arm, and every number after it inherits the error.

Worked, on the practice bracket

On the practice bracket, a load of 245.25 N hangs 440 mm from the centre of the bolt pattern.

M = F · d = 245.25 × 440 = 107 910 N·mm

Your turn, half done

A mechanic pushes down with 150 N on a spanner, 250 mm from the centre of the nut. Here F = 150 N and d = 250 mm. What moment turns the nut?

N·mm

M = F · d = 150 × 250 = 37 500 N·mm.

Your turn

A shop sign weighs 90 N and hangs 320 mm out from where its arm is bolted to the wall. What moment does it put on the bolts?

N·mm

M = F · d = 90 × 320 = 28 800 N·mm.

Check yourself

A load hole is 330 mm from the column face. The centre of the bolt pattern is 45 mm from the column face. Which lever arm do you use?

285 mm: from the centre of the bolt pattern to the load, which is the column-face distance minus the offset. The bracket is held at its bolts, so that is where the arm starts.
What you can do now: find the moment any force makes about any pivot, and say where the arm is measured from.

cantilever.title: The cantilever, and the drawing that tells the truth
steps:
A diving board. A balcony. A shelf bracket. Our wall bracket. Each is held firmly at one end and free at the other: a cantilever.

To see what a cantilever has to survive, engineers draw it alone: cut it free from the wall and replace the wall by what the wall does to it. That sketch is a free-body diagram, and it is the most useful drawing in mechanics, because it cannot hide a force.

What the wall does. Two things, and only two:

  • it pushes up with a force R, so the bracket does not fall;
  • it holds back a moment at the root, M, so the bracket does not rotate and swing down.

The bracket is still. So the pushes balance: R equals the load W. And the turns balance: the wall's M equals the load's turning effect. That second balance is the one that sizes the bracket.

= ·

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

M
the moment at the root, where the bracket is held, in N·mm
W
the load's weight, hanging at the tip, in N
L
the lever arm, from the centre of the bolt pattern to the load, in mm
R
the wall's upward push, equal to W

In one sentence

The wall must hold back the load's whole turning effect: the load times its distance from the root.

Where it comes from

Take moments about the root, the point where the bracket is held. Which forces have a lever arm about that point?

  • R acts at the root. Its arm is zero, so it turns nothing.
  • W acts at the tip, a distance L away. It turns the bracket with a moment W · L (lesson 3).

For the bracket to stay still, the wall must turn it back by exactly the same amount. So the moment at the root is M = W · L.

Cut the bracket anywhere else and only the part of L beyond the cut pushes on it. So the moment is largest at the root and zero at the tip. That is why brackets crack at the root, and why the root is where we size them.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. N × mm = N·mm, as every moment is.
  • Where is it biggest? At the root. Look at the triangle under the bracket in the picture: tall at the wall, nothing at the tip.
  • Twice as long, twice the moment. L appears once, not squared.

The trap

Borrowing a formula from a different beam. W · L / 2 is the load spread evenly along the bracket. W · L / 4 is a load in the middle of a beam resting on two supports. L² comes with a spread load too. Our load hangs at one point, at distance L, from a beam held at one end: M = W · L, nothing more.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket, steps 1 and 2 of the challenge in a row:

StepWorkingResult
1 · The loadW = m · g = 25 × 9.81245.25 N
2 · The root momentM = W · L = 245.25 × 440107 910 N·mm

Your turn, half done

A load of W = 205 N hangs at the tip of a bracket, L = 480 mm from the centre of its bolts. What moment must the bolts hold back at the root?

N·mm

M = W · L = 205 × 480 = 98 400 N·mm.

Your turn

The card's final, in two steps, just like the challenge. A water tank of 28 kg hangs from a wall bracket, 520 mm from the centre of its bolts.

Step 1: what force does the tank pull with?

N

W = m · g = 28 × 9.81 = 274.68 N.

Check yourself

Step 2: with that force at 520 mm, what is the moment at the root?

N·mm

M = W · L = 274.68 × 520 = 142 834 N·mm.

Check yourself

A classmate writes M = W · L / 2 for our bracket. Which bracket does that formula actually describe?

A load spread evenly along the length. Its weight acts, on average, halfway out, so its arm is L / 2. Ours hangs at the tip: the whole L.
What you can do now: draw a cantilever alone, name what the wall does to it, and find its root moment in N·mm. That is steps 1 and 2 of the wall bracket challenge, done.

stress.title: Force spread over an area
steps:
Hang a heavy bag from a thin string and it cuts into your fingers. Hang it from a wide strap and it doesn't. Same weight, same hand: the difference is how much material the force is shared over.

Steel works the same way. It doesn't care how big a force is. It cares how much force each little piece of it has to carry. That share is called stress, and it is the number a steel's strength is quoted in.

= / , = ·

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

σ
the stress: how hard each square millimetre is pulled, in MPa
F
the force the bar carries, in N
A
the area of steel the force is shared over, in mm²
b
the width of a flat bar, in mm
t
its thickness, in mm

In one sentence

Stress is the force divided by the area that carries it: the same pull on half the steel is twice the stress.

Where it comes from

Cut the bar anywhere across. The part below the cut still hangs there, so the steel across the cut must be holding up the whole force F. No single point holds it all: every square millimetre of the cut takes its share.

Share F newtons out over A square millimetres and each one carries F / A newtons. That share is the stress, σ.

For a flat bar the cut is a rectangle, b wide and t thick, so its area is A = b · t.

Why engineers like N and mm: one newton on one square millimetre is one megapascal, 1 MPa = 1 N/mm². Work in N and mm and the stress comes out directly in MPa, the unit every steel's strength is written in.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. N ÷ mm² = N/mm² = MPa.
  • Half the area, twice the stress. A is underneath: less steel, more stress.
  • Twice the force, twice the stress. F is on top.

The trap

The area in the wrong unit. One square metre is a million square millimetres. Put F in N over A in m² and you get pascals, a million times smaller than MPa, and a bar that looks a million times too strong. Keep N and mm, and the answer is in MPa.

And for a flat bar, multiply width and thickness. Adding them is a length, not an area.

Worked, on the practice bracket

Suppose the practice bracket's plate were not bent at all, but pulled straight by its load, like a hanger:

WorkingResult
The areaA = b · t = 30 × 8240 mm²
The stressσ = F / A = 245.25 / 2401.0219 MPa

About one megapascal, against a steel good for hundreds. Pulled straight, the plate would hardly notice the load. Keep that number in mind: Card 3 shows what bending does to it.

Your turn, half done

A flat bar 10 mm wide and 6 mm thick carries a pull of 1500 N. Its area is 10 × 6 mm². What is the stress?

MPa

σ = F / (b · t) = 1500 / (10 × 6) = 25 MPa.

Your turn

A tie bar 12 mm wide and 5 mm thick holds a sign with a pull of 2400 N. What stress is the steel carrying?

MPa

A = 12 × 5 mm², so σ = F / A = 2400 / A = 40 MPa.

Check yourself

The same bar, the same pull, but the bar is ground down to half its thickness. What happens to its stress?

It doubles. Half the thickness is half the area, so each square millimetre carries twice the share. The steel is the same; the load on each piece of it is not.
What you can do now: say what a stress is, and work one out in MPa from a force and an area. Next: how much stress a steel can take, and how much of that you should allow.

allowable.title: Yield, and why the safety factor goes on the steel
steps:
Bend a paper clip a little and let go: it springs back. Bend it a lot and it stays bent. Somewhere in between, the metal stopped behaving like a spring and started to flow.

Steel does exactly this. The stress at which it stops springing back is its yield strength, Re. A bracket that goes past it is not broken yet, but it is bent for good, and a bent bracket is a failed one.

= /

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

σ_allow
the allowable stress: the most you will let the steel carry, in MPa
Re
the yield strength: where the steel stops springing back, in MPa
n
the safety factor: how many times below yield you stay, no unit
σ
the stress in the steel, in MPa

In one sentence

You never design to the yield strength itself: you divide it by a safety factor and design to what is left.

Where it comes from

The picture is what a steel test shows. Pull a sample harder and harder: the stress σ climbs in a straight line while the steel still springs back. At Re the line goes flat, and the steel starts stretching without taking more load. Unload it now and it comes back along the dashed line: shorter than it was, but longer than it started. That is yield.

Why stay far below it? Because every number you design with is a little wrong: the real load, the real steel, the real plate, the hole someone drilled a millimetre off. The safety factor n is the room left for all of it. Divide Re by n and you get the stress you allow: σ_allow = Re / n.

Why on the steel and not on the load? Both are used in real practice. This path puts n on the material so that everyone's working has the same steps and each one can be checked (brief §6).

Check it makes sense

  • Units. MPa ÷ a pure number = MPa.
  • Bigger n, smaller σ_allow. More safety means you allow less, so the plate comes out thicker.
  • σ_allow is always below Re. A safety factor is more than 1.

The trap

Multiplying instead of dividing. Re × n is a stress above yield: a bracket designed to it bends the first day. If your allowable stress is bigger than Re, stop.

And the grade is in the name: S235, S275 and S355 are steels whose yield strength, for plates like ours, is at least the number in the name, in MPa. Different steel, different Re: read it off the brief, never from memory.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket is S275 steel with a safety factor of 2.5:

WorkingResult
Allowable stressσ_allow = Re / n = 275 / 2.5110 MPa

That is step 3 of the challenge, on the practice bracket.

Your turn, half done

A frame of S355 steel, Re = 355 MPa, is designed with a safety factor n = 2. Divide: what stress will you allow?

MPa

σ_allow = Re / n = 355 / 2 = 177.5 MPa.

Your turn

A lifting lug is made of S275, Re = 275 MPa. Lifting gear gets a bigger safety factor: n = 3. What is its allowable stress?

MPa

σ_allow = Re / n = 275 / 3 = 91.667 MPa.

Check yourself

A classmate does it the other way: multiplies the load by n, and compares the stress with the full Re. What happens to their bracket?

The same thickness. F × n against Re is the same comparison as F against Re / n. It is not wrong engineering, but the brief asks for the allowable stress as step 3, so their step answers would not line up with the ones the checker expects.
What you can do now: say what yield is, and turn a yield strength and a safety factor into an allowable stress. That is step 3 of the wall bracket challenge, done.

bending.title: How a plate carries a moment
steps:
Card 1 ended with a moment at the root, M, in N·mm. Card 2 ended with a stress the steel may carry, σ_allow, in MPa. This lesson joins them.

Bend a thick book: the pages on the outside of the curve slide out, the ones on the inside bunch up. A steel plate does the same. One edge is stretched, the other is squeezed, and a line through the middle is neither.

= / → = /

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

σ
the stress at the plate's top and bottom edge, in MPa
M
the bending moment the plate carries, in N·mm
Z
the section modulus: the plate's shape, as bending strength, in mm³
σ_allow
the allowable stress from Card 2, in MPa

In one sentence

The edge stress is the moment divided by the section modulus; to keep it at the allowable stress, the plate needs a section modulus of at least M / σ_allow.

Where it comes from

Look at the triangles in the picture. The stress is zero on the middle line and grows in a straight line to its largest, σ, at the two edges: stretching at the top, squeezing at the bottom. The edges are where the steel works hardest, so the edges are what we check.

How big is σ for a given moment? It depends on the moment, and on the shape of the section: how much steel there is, and how far from the middle it sits. Engineers wrap the shape into one number, the section modulus Z, so that σ = M / Z. The next lesson shows where Z comes from.

To design, turn it round. You know M (Card 1) and the stress you allow (Card 2). The plate must have a Z big enough that the edge stress stays at or below σ_allow: Z = M / σ_allow.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. N·mm ÷ MPa = N·mm ÷ (N/mm²) = mm³. A section modulus is always in mm³.
  • Twice the moment, twice the Z. A heavier load needs a stronger shape.
  • A lower σ_allow means a bigger Z. More safety, more steel.

The trap

Dividing the wrong way. σ_allow / M is a tiny number with no meaning. The moment goes on top: Z = M / σ_allow.

And mixing N·m with MPa. A moment in N·m over MPa gives a number a thousand times too small. Keep the moment in N·mm (Card 1, lesson 2).

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket, steps 2 and 3 into step 4:

WorkingResult
Root moment (step 2)Card 1107 910 N·mm
Allowable stress (step 3)Card 2110 MPa
Section modulus neededZ = M / σ_allow = 107 910 / 110981 mm³

Remember the plate pulled straight in Card 2: 1.0219 MPa. Bent by the same load, the 8 mm plate has Z = 1200 mm³, so its edge stress is σ = M / Z = 107 910 / 1200 = 89.925 MPa. Same load, same plate: bending is what makes a bracket work.

Your turn, half done

A shelf arm carries a moment of 64 000 N·mm. Its steel may carry 125 MPa. So Z = M / σ_allow = 64 000 / 125: what section modulus does it need?

mm³

Z = 64 000 / 125 = 512 mm³.

Your turn

Two steps, like the challenge. A sign bracket carries a moment of 88 000 N·mm. It is S275, Re = 275 MPa, with a safety factor of 2.

Step 1: what stress will you allow?

MPa

σ_allow = Re / n = 275 / 2 = 137.5 MPa.

Check yourself

Step 2: with that allowable stress, what section modulus must the bracket have?

mm³

Z = M / σ_allow = 88 000 / 137.5 = 640 mm³.

Check yourself

Our wall bracket holds its load off the free end. Which edge of the plate is stretched?

The top edge. The load pulls the free end down, so the bracket curves like a frown: the top is stretched and the bottom squeezed. Steel is as strong either way, so the check is the same; but it is the top edge, by the bolts, where a crack in a real bracket starts.
What you can do now: say what the stress in a bent plate looks like, and find the section modulus a plate needs from its moment and its allowable stress. That is step 4 of the wall bracket challenge.

section.title: Why depth counts twice
steps:
Take a plastic ruler. Bend it lying flat: easy. Turn it on its edge and bend it again: you can hardly move it. Same ruler, same plastic, same amount of it. The only thing that changed is which way it stands.

This lesson is about why, because the wall bracket is that ruler standing on edge, and getting it the wrong way round is the most common mistake on the challenge.

= · ² / 6

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

Z
the section modulus of a rectangle, in mm³
t
its thickness: the width across the bending, in mm
b
its depth: the dimension in the plane of the bending, in mm
T
the pull of the stretched half
C
the push of the squeezed half

In one sentence

A rectangle's bending strength grows with its thickness, and with the square of its depth.

Where it comes from

Follow the picture. The top half of the section is stretched, the bottom half squeezed, and the stress grows from zero at the middle to σ at each edge.

  • How hard each half pushes. On average the stress over a half is σ / 2, and a half has an area of t · b / 2. So each half pushes with T = C = σ / 2 · t · b / 2 = σ · t · b / 4.
  • How far apart the pushes are. A triangle's push acts a third of the way in from its wide end. So T and C sit 2b / 3 apart.
  • The moment they carry. A push times its distance: M = σ · t · b / 4 · 2b / 3 = σ · t · b² / 6.

So M = σ · Z, with Z = t · b² / 6. The depth b appears twice: once because a deeper plate has more steel pushing, once because the pushes sit further apart. That is why it is squared, and t is not.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. mm × mm² = mm³.
  • Twice the depth, four times the Z. Twice the thickness, only twice.
  • The ruler. On edge against flat, the ratio is (t · b²) / (b · t²) = b / t. A ruler six times wider than it is thick is six times stronger on edge.

The trap

The plate lying flat. b · t² / 6 is the formula with depth and thickness swapped: the bracket turned to lie flat, like the ruler you bent easily. On the practice plate it gives 320 mm³ instead of 1200 mm³, weaker by b / t. The brief's edge view exists only to stop this: b is the dimension in the plane of the load.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice plate, 30 mm deep, at the 8 mm thickness strength chose:

WorkingResult
On edge, as it is boltedZ = t · b² / 6 = 8 × 30² / 61200 mm³
Lying flat, the trapb · t² / 6 = 30 × 8² / 6320 mm³

It needs 981 mm³ (lesson 1). On edge the plate has more than that; lying flat it would have far less.

Your turn, half done

A plate 10 mm thick and 40 mm deep stands on edge. Z = t · b² / 6 = 10 × 40² / 6. Finish it.

mm³

40² = 40 × 40; times 10, over 6: 2667 mm³.

Your turn

A lintel plate stands on edge: 50 mm deep, 12 mm thick. What is its section modulus?

mm³

Z = t · b² / 6 = 12 × 50² / 6 = 5000 mm³.

Check yourself

A steel strip 30 mm wide and 6 mm thick is bent first on edge, then flat. On edge, how much stronger is it?

5 times. On edge Z = t · b² / 6, flat Z = b · t² / 6; divide one by the other and b / t = 30 / 6 is left.
What you can do now: say why a plate on edge is so much stronger than a plate lying flat, and work out its section modulus. Next: turn the section modulus you need into a plate you can buy.

thickness.title: Sizing the plate, and buying steel that exists
steps: You know the section modulus the bracket needs (lesson 1) and what a plate's section modulus is (lesson 2). The drawing fixes the depth b. One thing is left to choose: the thickness t.

= 6 · / ²

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

t
the thickness that gives exactly the section modulus needed, in mm
Z
the section modulus needed, from lesson 1, in mm³
b
the plate's depth, fixed by the drawing, in mm

In one sentence

Turn the section modulus round to find the thickness, then buy the next plate up that a workshop actually stocks.

Where it comes from

Start from Z = t · b² / 6. Multiply both sides by 6 and divide both by b²: t = 6 · Z / b².

That t is the thickness that is exactly strong enough, and it is almost never a thickness you can buy. Steel plate comes in fixed sizes; the brief lists the ones stocked locally. So you buy the next size up. Every size below it has less Z than the bracket needs, however close it looks.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. mm³ ÷ mm² = mm.
  • A deeper plate needs less thickness, and by the square: b² is underneath.
  • The bought plate is never thinner than the formula's. If it is, you rounded the wrong way.

The trap

Rounding to the nearest. When the formula's thickness sits just over a stock size, the size below looks close enough. It is not: it is short of the strength you just worked out. Always up.

And forgetting the square: dividing by b instead of b² gives a thickness b times too big.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket, steps 5 and 6:

WorkingResult
Thickness neededt = 6 · Z / b² = 6 × 981 / 30²6.54 mm
Thickness boughtthe next stock size up8 mm

Your turn, half done

A plate 40 mm deep needs a section modulus of 3000 mm³. So t = 6 × 3000 / 40². What thickness is exactly enough?

mm

6 × 3000 / (40 × 40) = 11.25 mm.

Your turn

Two steps, like the challenge. A bracket 45 mm deep needs a section modulus of 1800 mm³.

Step 1: what thickness is exactly enough?

mm

t = 6 · Z / b² = 6 × 1800 / 45² = 5.3333 mm.

Check yourself

Step 2: the workshop stocks 6, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 mm plate. Which one do you buy?

mm

The next size up from 5.3333 mm: 6 mm.

Check yourself

Strength needs t = 8.1 mm. The stock is 6, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 mm. Which plate do you buy?

10 mm, the next size up. 8 mm is short of the strength you need, however little. 12 mm is not wrong steel, but it is not what the numbers ask for: the safety factor is already in σ_allow, and a second one, added by eye, is heavier and dearer for nothing. (Card 4 may still send you up a size, for stiffness. That is a reason worked out, not a guess.)

What you can do now: turn a section modulus into a thickness, and buy a plate that exists. That is steps 5 and 6 of the wall bracket challenge: the plate is strong enough. Card 4 asks whether strong is enough.

sag.title: Strong is not stiff
steps:
A diving board is strong: it carries a diver a thousand times and never breaks. It is also not stiff: it bends a long way, which is the whole point of it.

A bracket is the opposite. Strength (Card 3) says it will not bend for good. It says nothing about how far it bends while loaded: a bracket can be perfectly strong and still sag enough to tilt the hoist and swing the chain off line. This lesson measures the sag.

= · ³ / (3 · · )

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

δ
the tip deflection: how far the tip drops under the load, in mm
W
the load at the tip, in N
L
the lever arm, from the centre of the bolts to the load, in mm
E
Young's modulus: how stiff the steel itself is, in MPa
I
the second moment of area: how stiff the shape is, t · b³ / 12 for our plate, in mm⁴

In one sentence

The tip drops more for a heavier load and much more for a longer arm, and less for stiffer steel and a stiffer shape.

Where it comes from

Three things, each worth knowing on its own.

  • E, the steel's stiffness. How much stress it takes to stretch steel by a given share of its length. It is the slope of the straight line in Card 2's picture, and it is the same for every structural steel: S355 is stronger than S235, but not stiffer. The brief gives E = 210 000 MPa.
  • I, the shape's stiffness. Close cousin of Z: I = Z · b / 2, which is t · b³ / 12 for a rectangle. One more b than Z, because for stiffness a fibre far from the middle counts once for its push, once for its lever, and once more for how far it stretches.
  • L³, the length three times over. The moment grows with L (Card 1). The plate bends along all of L. And the small angle it turns through at the root is carried out a distance L to the tip. Three Ls. The 3 underneath comes from adding the bending up along a moment that falls from W · L at the root to nothing at the tip: take that one on trust here.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. N · mm³ ÷ (MPa · mm⁴) = N · mm³ ÷ (N/mm² · mm⁴) = mm.
  • Twice as long, eight times the sag. L is cubed. Long brackets are usually decided by stiffness, not strength.
  • Twice as deep, an eighth of the sag. Twice as thick, only half.

The trap

E in GPa. Books often print steel's E in gigapascals. Put that number into a formula where everything else is in N and mm and E is a thousand times too small, so the sag is a thousand times too big. In N and mm, E is in MPa: 210 000.

And I with b and t swapped, the plate lying flat again: it is wrong by (b / t)², far worse than the factor it cost in Z.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket at the 8 mm plate strength chose, step 7:

WorkingResult
The shapeI = t · b³ / 12 = 8 × 30³ / 1218 000 mm⁴
The sagδ = W · L³ / (3 · E · I) = 245.25 × 440³ / (3 × 210 000 × 18 000)1.8423 mm

Under two millimetres. Is that a lot? The next lesson says.

Your turn, half done

A load of 300 N at the tip of a plate 400 mm long, 40 mm deep and 8 mm thick. Set up for you: I = 8 × 40³ / 12, and δ = 300 × 400³ / (3 × 210 000 × I). Finish it: how far does the tip drop?

mm

I = 8 × 40³ / 12 mm⁴, and then δ = 0.71429 mm.

Your turn

A steel bracket, 45 mm deep and 10 mm thick, carries 520 N at its tip, 550 mm from the centre of its bolts. How far does the tip sag?

mm

I = t · b³ / 12 = 10 × 45³ / 12, then δ = W · L³ / (3 · E · I) = 1.8084 mm.

Check yourself

The same plate and the same load, but the bracket is made twice as long. How much further does the tip sag?

Eight times. L is cubed: 2 × 2 × 2. Its moment doubles, it bends over twice the length, and it carries its root angle twice as far.
What you can do now: say why a strong bracket can still be too bendy, and work out how far its tip sags. That is step 7 of the wall bracket challenge.

limit.title: Two checks, one answer
steps: You can now work out two things about a plate: whether it is strong enough (Card 3) and how far it sags (lesson 1). The last question is how far is too far, and what to do when the plate strength chose sags past it.

= / 300

Tap a symbol to find it in the drawing.

δ_limit
the most the tip may sag, in mm
L
the lever arm, from the centre of the bolts to the load, in mm
δ
the tip deflection you worked out, in mm

In one sentence

The tip may sag no more than the bracket's length divided by 300; the plate you use is the thinnest one that is strong enough and stays within that.

Where it comes from

This limit is not about breaking. It is a serviceability limit: a promise about how the part behaves in use. A sag you can see makes people distrust a bracket; a hoist on a sagging arm hangs its chain off line; whatever is fixed to a bendy part cracks. Design codes set limits of this kind, tighter or looser depending on what is attached, as a share of the span. This brief chooses L / 300.

So a plate has two checks, and it must pass both:

  1. strong enough: its thickness is at least the one Card 3 found;
  2. stiff enough: its sag δ is at most δ_limit.

The walk: start at the plate strength chose. Work out its δ. If δ ≤ δ_limit, that is your plate. If not, take the next stock size up and work out δ again. The first plate that passes both checks is the answer to step 8.

Check it makes sense

  • Units. mm ÷ a pure number = mm.
  • A longer bracket may sag more, but not much more. δ_limit grows with L; the sag grows with L³. The longer the arm, the likelier stiffness decides.
  • The answer is never thinner than step 6. Stiffness can only send you up the list.

The trap

Stopping at step 6. Strength chose a plate, and it is tempting to call it done. On roughly one set of numbers in three, the sag decides instead, and step 8 is a bigger plate.

And "close enough" again. A sag a hair over the limit is over. The practice bracket below misses at one size by less than one per cent.

Worked, on the practice bracket

The practice bracket. The limit first: δ_limit = 440 / 300 = 1.4667 mm. Then the walk up the stock list:

PlateIts sag δWithin 1.4667 mm?
8 mm, strength's choice1.8423 mmno
10 mm1.4738 mmno, by a hair
12 mm1.2282 mmyes

So the practice bracket uses 12 mm plate, not the 8 mm strength asked for. Stiffness decided.

Your turn, half done

A bracket's load hangs 450 mm from the centre of its bolts, and δ_limit = 450 / 300: how far may its tip sag?

mm

450 / 300 = 1.5 mm.

Your turn

The card's final. A bracket 48 mm deep carries 650 N at 560 mm. Strength alone needs 7.2 mm of thickness. The stock is 6, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 mm.

Walk up the list from the first plate strong enough: which thickness do you use?

mm

δ_limit = 560 / 300 mm. Strength says 8 mm; at 8 mm and at 10 mm the tip sags past the limit, and at 12 mm it does not. Stiffness decided.

Check yourself

For one bracket, strength asks for 8 mm and stiffness for 12 mm. Which plate goes on the column?

12 mm. A plate is used only if it passes both checks. 8 mm is strong but bendy; 10 mm is not a compromise, it simply fails the stiffness check.

What you can do now: say what a deflection limit is for, and pick the thinnest stock plate that is both strong and stiff enough. That is steps 7 and 8, and the whole calculation of the wall bracket challenge.
